extracted.intended_audience: students of geometry / mathematics undergraduates and advanced secondary students studying classical ruler-and-compass constructions and field-theoretic characterization of constructible numbers
extracted.subtask_description: Theory and practical rules for performing and analysing Euclidean ruler-and-compass constructions, including which numerical quantities are constructible, the allowed elementary steps, and algebraic criteria (field extensions by square roots) for constructibility and impossibility results (doubling cube, trisecting angle, regular heptagon, squaring the circle).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction of a geometrical construction to algebraic problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Any geometrical construction problem can be formulated as: a certain set of line segments a, b, c, ... is given and one or more other segments x, y, ... are sought; the geometrical construction amounts to (1) finding a relationship (equation) between the required quantity x and the given quantities, (2) solving this equation for x, and (3) determining whether this solution can be obtained by the proposed constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate geometric constraints into algebraic equations (e.g. coordinates, similarity relations). After solving the algebraic equation, check whether the solution can be realized by the permitted ruler-and-compass steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowed elementary construction steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Every ruler-and-compass construction consists of a sequence of steps, each of which is one of the following: 1) connecting two points by a straight line, 2) finding the point of intersection of two lines, 3) drawing a circle with a given radius about a point, 4) finding the points of intersection of a circle with another circle or with a line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat any element (point, line, circle) as known if it was given or constructed previously. All analysis of constructibility must respect these primitive operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitted 'arbitrary' choices may be taken rational
rubrics_metrics.description: When arbitrary elements appear (arbitrary lines, points or radii) we may choose them to be rational: arbitrary points with rational coordinates, arbitrary lines ax+by+c=0 with rational coefficients, arbitrary circles with rational centers and radii.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Making arbitrary choices rational does not affect constructibility results, and simplifies algebraic analysis by keeping the base field rational.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic algebraic operations are geometrically constructible
rubrics_metrics.description: From two given segments of lengths a and b we can construct a + b, a − b, p a (for integer p), a/q (for integer q), and ab; equivalently addition, subtraction, multiplication and division of known quantities can be performed by geometrical constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete constructions: mark lengths on a line for sums/differences; use parallel lines and similar triangles to construct rational multiples and divisions; use similarity (and chord constructions) to multiply and divide lengths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of square roots
rubrics_metrics.description: The decisive new construction beyond the rational field is the extraction of a square root: if a segment a is given then √a can be constructed using only ruler and compass (circle with diameter OB where OA = a and AB = 1, perpendicular through A meets circle at C, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the semicircle/right-triangle method (angle in semicircle is right) to obtain AC = √a; square-root extraction is the single non-rational primitive that extends the field of constructible numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number field generated by given quantities
rubrics_metrics.description: The totality of quantities obtainable from given segments a, b, c, ... by repeated application of addition, subtraction, multiplication and division constitutes a number field: a set closed under the four rational operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Call the field generated by the given numbers the base field (e.g. rational numbers if a single unit segment is given). All 'rational' constructions remain inside this field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructible numbers as successive quadratic extensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructible numbers are exactly those obtainable from the initial field F0 by a finite sequence of extension fields Fi where each extension is formed by adjoining a square root √ki (ki in Fi−1 but √ki not in Fi−1); after n adjunctions we obtain a field Fn and all numbers in Fn are constructible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently, constructible numbers are those lying in some tower of quadratic extensions over the initial field; the number of adjunctions measures complexity but is finite for constructible lengths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of ruler-only operations on fields
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of the ruler alone (drawing lines through known points and finding their intersections) cannot take us beyond the current field F: coefficients of line equations and intersection formulas remain in F, so coordinates of new points lie in F.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show algebraically by writing line equations with coefficients in F and solving linear systems; this justifies that only compass (circle intersections) can introduce square roots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of compass operations: quadratic equations / adjunctions of square roots
rubrics_metrics.description: Intersection of a circle with a line or of two circles leads to solving a quadratic equation whose coefficients lie in the current field F, and thus produces new coordinates of the form p + q√k with p,q,k in F (i.e. one quadratic extension).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eliminate y to get Ax^2 + Bx + C = 0 with A,B,C in F and apply quadratic formula; this shows a single compass step can only adjoin a single square root.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization: all constructible numbers are algebraic of degree 2^n
rubrics_metrics.description: If the initial field F0 is the rational field, then all constructible numbers are algebraic; numbers in a field Fk (after k square-root adjunctions) are roots of polynomial equations of degree 2^k with rational coefficients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use induction: each adjunction doubles the maximum algebraic degree; concretely, numbers in Fi satisfy quadratic equations over Fi−1 and hence ultimately a degree-2^k polynomial over Q.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method for proving impossibility of classical Greek problems
rubrics_metrics.description: To show a classical construction is impossible (doubling the cube, trisecting a general angle, constructing regular heptagon) demonstrate the target length/number would require an algebraic degree not a power of two (or otherwise not attainable by successive square-root adjunctions) — typically by showing the defining polynomial is irreducible of degree not 2^n or by contradiction with minimality of the extension tower.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in text: x^3 − 2 for doubling the cube (cube root of 2 cannot lie in any tower of quadratic extensions), certain cubics for trisecting angle, and y^3+y^2−2y−1 for the regular heptagon. Use rational-root/degree arguments to rule out membership in any quadratic tower.

rubrics_metrics.name: Squaring the circle and transcendence criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Squaring the circle is impossible with ruler and compass because it would require constructing a segment of length √π, which would mean π is algebraic; but π is transcendental (Lindemann), so it cannot belong to any field obtained by successive adjunctions of square roots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conclude impossibility from the fact that all elements of any finite tower of quadratic extensions are algebraic, while π is transcendental; historical remark: Lindemann proved π transcendental (beyond scope of elementary geometry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructibility of regular polygons via nested square roots and doubling
rubrics_metrics.description: Many regular polygons (e.g., 2^n-gons, hexagon, decagon → pentagon via decagon alternation) can be constructed by repeated arc-bisection (doubling the number of sides) and by operations leading to expressions with nested square roots; explicit formula for side of 2n-gon involves n−1 nested square roots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use chord-length relations and the doubling formula s_{2n} = √(2 − √(4 − s_n^2)) to generate successive constructible side lengths; show that sides of polygons like 5·2^n, 3·2^n are obtainable by additions and square-root extractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of algebraic/formulaic checks to verify constructibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an explicit length expression, verify constructibility by exhibiting a finite sequence of adjunctions of square roots (i.e., write the number in nested √-form or demonstrate it satisfies a polynomial whose degree is a power of two coming from a quadratic tower).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises provided: represent composite radicals in the standard extension-field form (p + q√k with p,q,k in previous field) and determine the sequence of fields Fi that produce a desired value (e.g., side of regular 2^m-gon).

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometrical transformations (inversion) as systematic tools for constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Many construction problems are clarified or simplified by considering classes of problems connected by geometrical transformations (e.g., inversion in a circle is a generalization of reflection and can be used to reframe and solve construction problems).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approach problems by mapping them under transformations to simpler equivalent problems (this is a general method rather than a primitive operation; specifics are developed in subsequent sections).
